title: From Voice to Page: Collection, Script and Tajwid
bigQuestion: How did words first spoken aloud in Arabia become the written Qur'an that Muslims recite today, and how do we know?

story.title: Two Pages Older Than Anyone Thought
story.kicker: In a university library in England, two sheets of parchment turn out to be among the oldest Qur'an pages in the world.
paragraphs: The University of Birmingham keeps a collection of old Middle Eastern manuscripts gathered in the 1920s. For decades, two leaves of parchment sat filed with a later Qur'an manuscript. The writing on them was Arabic, in a tall, slanted early style with almost no dots. A researcher working on her doctorate, Alba Fedeli, looked closely and thought the two leaves did not belong with the pages around them. They looked older.

The library sent a tiny piece of the parchment to a radiocarbon lab at Oxford. Radiocarbon dating measures how much of a certain kind of carbon is left in something that was once alive, like the animal skin that became parchment. In 2015 the result came back. With about 95 percent probability, the animal whose skin made the pages had died between 568 and 645 CE. That range overlaps the lifetime of Muhammad, who died in 632.

The text on the two leaves is parts of Surahs 18, 19 and 20. When scholars compared it with the standard printed Qur'an, the wording matched, though the old pages had no vowel marks and few dots, and the verse divisions were shown with simple clusters of strokes. Newspapers around the world ran the story. The library put the pages on display, and thousands came to see them, many of them Muslims from Birmingham's large Muslim community.

Scholars were careful about what the date proved. Radiocarbon dates the skin, not the ink. A scribe could have written on older parchment. Some argued the pages were made a little later than the range suggests, based on the script. But most agreed the leaves were from the first decades of Islam and that they showed a text close to the one Muslims read today. The find did not settle every question. It gave everyone, believers and historians alike, something solid to look at.
story.think: Radiocarbon dating tells us when the animal died, not when the words were written. What else would you want to know before saying how old the text on the pages is?

lessons.title: A Recitation Before a Book
lessons.mainIdea: The word Qur'an means recitation; Muslims say its words were spoken and heard for years before they were gathered into a single written book.
reading: The name of the book is a clue to what it was first. *Qur'an* comes from an Arabic root meaning to recite or read aloud. Muslim tradition says the first word revealed to Muhammad was a command to recite: Iqra (96:1). For the roughly 23 years that followed, by that tradition, the words came in pieces and were spoken aloud, learned by heart and repeated. Writing came alongside, but hearing came first.

The Qur'an describes itself as something recited. It calls itself a Reminder and says it was sent down in stages so it could be recited to people slowly (17:106). It tells the Prophet to recite it in measured tones (73:4). It refers to itself being read in the dawn prayer (17:78). These verses are one reason Muslims say the Qur'an is meant to be heard, not only read silently on a page.

In Arabia around 600, most poetry and tribal history lived in memory and voice. Historians note that Arabic writing existed, but writing was used mostly for contracts, letters and short inscriptions. A community used to memorizing long poems was well prepared to memorize a text. That does not mean nothing was written. It means writing was a support for the voice, not the other way round.

This shapes how Muslims use the book today. A person who reads the Qur'an aloud is doing what the word means. A printed copy is called a *mushaf*, a word for a bound collection of pages, to mark the difference between the sound and the object. The sound is the Qur'an. The mushaf is where it is written down.

words.d: the name of the book; the Arabic word means 'recitation' or 'reading aloud'
a written or printed copy of the Qur'an, as distinct from the recited text
'Recite!' or 'Read!', the first word of 96:1, which Muslim tradition calls the first revelation

look.title: The First Word
look.text: Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth, Createth man from a clot. Read: And thy Lord is the Most Bounteous, Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not.
look.cite: Qur'an 96:1–5, Surah Al-Alaq (The Clot), trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: The passage opens with a command to read and then praises teaching by the pen. What does that pairing suggest about voice and writing in the Qur'an's own view of itself?

check.q: What does the word Qur'an mean?
check.why: Qur'an comes from a root meaning to recite; mushaf is the word for the written copy.

check.q: What is a mushaf?
choices: a written or printed copy of the Qur'an
check.why: A mushaf is the bound written text; the Qur'an in Muslim usage is the recited word.

check.q: In Arabia around 600, historians say writing was mostly used for
check.why: Arabic writing existed but poetry and history lived mainly in memory and voice.

lessons.title: Memorizers and Scribes
lessons.mainIdea: In the Prophet's lifetime, by Muslim tradition, companions memorized the Qur'an and scribes wrote pieces of it on whatever they had, so the text lived in two forms at once.
reading: Muslim tradition names people who learned the whole text by heart in the Prophet's lifetime. Such a person is called a *hafiz*, a guardian. Reports in the hadith collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim name several, including Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Zayd ibn Thabit. The Prophet, tradition says, would recite each year's revelation with the angel Jibril (Gabriel) during Ramadan, and twice in his final year.

Alongside the memorizers were scribes. Tradition reports that the Prophet dictated verses to companions who wrote them on what was available: pieces of parchment, flat stones, the shoulder blades of camels, the ribs of palm leaves. Zayd ibn Thabit, a young man from Medina, is named as a chief scribe. Historians cannot check each report, but they generally accept that some writing took place during the Prophet's life, since Arabic writing was in use.

What did not exist yet, by all accounts, was one complete bound book with the surahs in order. The pieces were spread among many people and objects. When someone asked what the Qur'an said, the answer lived in the memory of the huffaz (plural of hafiz) and in scattered written sheets that could be checked against them. Memory and writing checked each other.

This double life is the key to what came next. When a written copy was finally gathered, the collectors did not simply copy sheets. Tradition says they required both a written piece and the testimony of those who had heard it from the Prophet. A student can see why: a book that lives in voices needs the voices to vouch for the pages.

words.d: a person who has memorized the whole Qur'an; plural huffaz; the word means guardian
a companion of the Prophet named by tradition as a chief scribe and later as head of the collection
a person who writes down a text; early scribes wrote Qur'an verses on parchment, stones and palm ribs

look.title: Two Ways to Keep a Text
look.text: Imagine a poem that only ten people in a town know by heart, and that is also written on scraps kept in twenty different houses. No one has the whole thing on paper. If a scrap is lost, the memorizers still have it. If a memorizer misremembers a line, the scraps can be checked.
look.prompt: What are the strengths and the risks of keeping a text in memory and in scattered writing at the same time? Which risk would worry you most?

check.q: What is a hafiz?
choices: a scribe who writes the Qur'an
a person who has memorized the whole Qur'an
check.why: Hafiz means guardian and names one who knows the whole text by heart.

check.q: By tradition, on what did early scribes write Qur'an verses?
choices: clay tablets fired in a kiln
parchment, stones, camel shoulder blades and palm ribs
check.why: Reports name parchment, flat stones, shoulder blades and palm-leaf ribs, whatever was at hand.

check.q: Which of these did NOT exist during the Prophet's lifetime, according to Muslim tradition and historians?
choices: a scribe named Zayd ibn Thabit
one complete bound book of all the surahs in order
check.why: The text lived in memory and scattered writings; a single complete book came after the Prophet's death.

lessons.title: Abu Bakr's Collection
lessons.mainIdea: Muslim tradition says the first caliph, Abu Bakr, had the Qur'an gathered into one set of sheets after many memorizers died in battle, c. 633.
reading: The Prophet Muhammad died in 632. Abu Bakr, his close companion, became the first *caliph*, the leader of the Muslim community. Within a year, by tradition, the Muslims fought a hard battle at Yamama in central Arabia against a rival claiming prophethood. Many companions who had memorized the Qur'an were killed. A well-known report in al-Bukhari's collection tells what happened next.

In that report, Umar ibn al-Khattab went to Abu Bakr and urged him to gather the Qur'an before more huffaz died and parts were lost. Abu Bakr hesitated, saying the Prophet had not done this. Umar pressed him, and Abu Bakr agreed. He called Zayd ibn Thabit and gave him the task. Zayd, the report says, at first felt that moving a mountain would have been easier, but he set to work.

Zayd collected the text from written pieces and from the memories of the companions. Tradition says he required both kinds of evidence. The result was a set of sheets, called suhuf. They were kept with Abu Bakr, then with Umar. After Umar's death they went to his daughter Hafsa, who had been a wife of the Prophet. It was a reference copy, not a book sent out to the community.

Historians treat this account with respect and with caution. It comes from reports written down a century or more after the events, and the details vary between versions. Most scholars accept that some early collection took place under the first caliphs. What they debate is how complete and how official the collection was, and how much the standard text owes to this stage versus the next one.

words.d: the leader of the Muslim community after the Prophet's death; Abu Bakr was the first
a battle in central Arabia, c. 633, in which tradition says many memorizers of the Qur'an died
loose sheets; the name given to the collection made under Abu Bakr and kept by Hafsa

look.title: Moving a Mountain
look.text: In a report preserved by al-Bukhari, Zayd ibn Thabit says that when Abu Bakr asked him to collect the Qur'an, he felt that being told to move a mountain would have been lighter than this task. He then gathered the text from palm ribs, flat stones and the memories of the people.
look.cite: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an, report of Zayd ibn Thabit on the collection under Abu Bakr; paraphrased
look.prompt: Zayd says the task felt heavier than moving a mountain. What would have made it so hard, given how the text was kept until then?

check.q: Who does tradition say urged Abu Bakr to collect the Qur'an?
check.why: In al-Bukhari's report, Umar pressed Abu Bakr after the losses at Yamama.

check.q: Where were the sheets of Abu Bakr's collection kept after Umar's death?
check.why: Tradition says the suhuf passed from Abu Bakr to Umar to Hafsa.

check.q: How do historians generally treat the account of Abu Bakr's collection?
choices: They accept that an early collection likely took place while debating the details
check.why: The reports are late and vary, so scholars accept the outline while debating how complete and official it was.

lessons.title: Uthman's Standard Copy
lessons.mainIdea: Around 650, by Muslim tradition, the caliph Uthman had a standard copy made, sent copies to major cities and ordered other versions destroyed, giving the text one form.
reading: Uthman ibn Affan became the third caliph in 644. By then Muslims lived from Egypt to Persia. Reports in al-Bukhari tell of a commander named Hudhayfa returning from a campaign. He was alarmed to hear Muslims from different regions arguing over how to recite the Qur'an. He asked Uthman to act before the community split over its scripture. Earlier communities, he said, had split that way.

Uthman, tradition says, borrowed the sheets from Hafsa. He appointed a committee led by Zayd ibn Thabit, with three men from the tribe of Quraysh, to make copies. Where the men differed, the text was to follow the dialect of Quraysh, the Prophet's tribe. The copies were finished around 650. Uthman sent one to each major center, such as Kufa, Basra and Damascus, and kept one in Medina. He ordered that other written versions be burned.

This is the moment Muslims call the standardization of the text, and the copies are called the *Uthmanic codex*. Some companions, notably Abdullah ibn Mas'ud in Kufa, are reported to have been unhappy at first, since their own copies differed in the order of surahs and in some readings. Over time the Uthmanic text won general acceptance. Sunni and Shia Muslims today read the same Uthmanic text.

Historians ask what exactly the early copies looked like and how much later hands touched them. The oldest surviving manuscripts are from the seventh century. They match the Uthmanic text closely in wording, which supports the tradition's outline. The early script had no dots and vowels. That left room for slight differences in reading. Those differences became the subject of a whole science, taken up later in this chapter.

words.d: the third caliph, ruled 644 to 656; tradition says he had the standard copy of the Qur'an made c. 650
the standard written text made under Uthman and sent to the main Muslim cities
the tribe of Mecca to which the Prophet belonged; the standard copy followed its dialect

look.title: From Voice to Standard Text
rows: Battle of Yamama; Abu Bakr's collection begins
look.cite: Dates as Muslim tradition gives them, in the sira and in reports preserved by al-Bukhari; historians treat those before 632 as approximate
look.prompt: How many years passed between the Prophet's death and the standard copy? Why might that gap matter to a historian, and why might it not to a Muslim reader?

check.q: Who does tradition say asked Uthman to standardize the text?
check.why: Hudhayfa reported disputes among soldiers over recitation and urged Uthman to act.

check.q: What did Uthman do with the standard copies?
choices: sent one to each major city and ordered other versions burned
check.why: Copies went to centers like Kufa, Basra and Damascus, and other written versions were to be destroyed.

check.q: Which companion is reported to have objected at first to the Uthmanic copy?
check.why: Ibn Mas'ud in Kufa had his own copy that differed in surah order and some readings.

lessons.title: Old Manuscripts Speak
lessons.mainIdea: Early Qur'an manuscripts, such as the Birmingham leaves radiocarbon-dated to the seventh century, let historians check the tradition against physical evidence.
reading: For most of history, what we knew about the early Qur'an text came from Muslim reports. In the past few decades, scientists have added a new kind of evidence: the parchment itself. *Radiocarbon dating* measures the decay of a form of carbon in anything that was once alive. Parchment is animal skin, so it can be dated. The method gives a range, not a single year, and it dates the skin, not the writing.

The Birmingham leaves are the best-known case. Two folios, catalogued as Mingana 1572a, hold parts of Surahs 18 to 20. In 2015 the University of Birmingham announced a radiocarbon date of 568 to 645 CE with 95.4 percent probability. The script is *Hijazi*, an early Arabic hand that slants to the right, with almost no dots. Scholars connected the leaves to a manuscript in Paris written in the same hand.

Other early manuscripts sit in Istanbul, Cairo, St. Petersburg, Paris and Tübingen. A folio in Tübingen was dated to 649 to 675 CE with 95 percent probability. Together they show that by the mid-seventh century, the Qur'an was being copied on large, carefully prepared parchment in a text that matches the standard reading in wording, though not in spelling conventions, dots or vowel marks.

What these finds do not do is settle every debate. A date range that begins before the Prophet's death does not mean the pages were written then. The skin may have been prepared and used later. Historians and Muslim scholars both point this out. What the manuscripts give is a floor: the text Muslims read today was already on parchment within a generation or two of the events tradition describes.

words.d: a method that dates once-living material, like parchment, by measuring carbon decay; gives a range of years
an early Arabic writing style, slanted and with few dots, used in the oldest Qur'an manuscripts
one leaf of a manuscript, written on both sides

look.title: Radiocarbon Ranges for Early Leaves
look.cite: University of Birmingham radiocarbon announcement, 2015 (95.4% probability); University of Tübingen announcement, 2014 (95% probability)
look.prompt: A range is not a date. What is the earliest and latest the Birmingham skin could be from, and why is that both exciting and limiting?

check.q: What does radiocarbon dating measure in a parchment page?
choices: the age of the animal skin
check.why: Radiocarbon dates once-living material, so it dates the skin, not the writing on it.

check.q: What text is on the Birmingham leaves?
check.why: Mingana 1572a holds portions of Al-Kahf, Maryam and Ta Ha, Surahs 18 to 20.

check.q: Why do scholars say the 568 to 645 range does not prove the pages were written in the Prophet's lifetime?
choices: Because the pages are in Latin
Because the skin could have been prepared and written on later
Because radiocarbon is never used on parchment
check.why: The date is for the animal's death; a scribe could have used the parchment some years afterward.

lessons.title: The Sana'a Palimpsest
lessons.mainIdea: A manuscript found in Yemen in 1972 has an erased lower text with some differences from the standard Qur'an, giving scholars a rare look at an early non-standard copy.
reading: In 1972, workers repairing the roof of the Great Mosque of Sana'a, the capital of Yemen, found a hidden chamber packed with old manuscript pages. Among them were pieces of what may be the oldest Qur'an manuscripts known. One set of leaves is a *palimpsest*: parchment that was written on, scraped or washed off, and written on again. The upper text is a normal early Qur'an. The lower, faint text is the surprise.

The lower text, made visible with ultraviolet light and careful study, is also the Qur'an, but with differences. Words are sometimes added, dropped or replaced by near-synonyms, and in a few places the order of verses or surahs differs from the standard. Radiocarbon tests place the parchment in the seventh century, most likely before about 671 CE. Scholars have published editions of parts of it since the 2000s.

What does it show? Most scholars read the lower text as one of the companion copies that Muslim tradition itself describes, the kind that Uthman's standard copy replaced. In that reading, it confirms the tradition: there were early variant copies, and they were set aside. The differences are real but limited. The surahs, the stories and the message are the same. Some scholars draw larger conclusions about how fluid the early text was. Others caution that one palimpsest is a small sample.

For students, the Sana'a find is a good example of how evidence and tradition talk to each other. Muslim reports said non-standard copies once existed. A manuscript turned up that looks like one. That the upper text is standard, written over the old one, is itself a picture of what the tradition describes: one text winning out and being written on top of the rest.

words.d: a manuscript page whose first writing was scraped off and written over; the faint lower text can sometimes be read
early Qur'an leaves found in the Great Mosque of Sana'a, Yemen, in 1972, including a palimpsest with a variant lower text

look.title: Reading What Was Erased
look.text: On one Sana'a leaf, the upper text reads like the standard Qur'an. Under ultraviolet light, a faint lower text appears. In one spot the lower text has an extra word; in another, a different word with nearly the same meaning; in a third, the same verse in a different place in the surah. The scribe who wrote the upper text was writing over a Qur'an that was already old.
look.prompt: Suppose you found this page. What would you conclude about how the early text was kept, and what would you be careful NOT to conclude from one page?

check.q: What is a palimpsest?
choices: a manuscript written over an erased earlier text
a set of dots on letters
check.why: The Sana'a palimpsest has an early Qur'an under a later one on the same parchment.

check.q: Where and when was the Sana'a manuscript found?
choices: the Great Mosque of Sana'a, Yemen, 1972
check.why: Workers repairing the mosque roof found the manuscripts in a hidden chamber in 1972.

check.q: How do most scholars read the lower text's differences?
choices: as one of the early companion copies that the Uthmanic text replaced
check.why: The variants fit tradition's own account of pre-Uthmanic companion copies with limited differences.

lessons.title: Dots and Vowel Marks
lessons.mainIdea: Early Arabic script had few dots and no vowel signs; over the first Islamic centuries, scholars added marks so readers who did not already know the text could read it correctly.
reading: Look at the Birmingham leaves and you see a problem. Arabic letters share shapes. The letters for b, t, th, n and y look alike and are told apart by dots above or below. Early Qur'an manuscripts have very few of these dots. They also have no vowel marks, the short signs for a, i and u that sit above and below letters. A reader who already knew the text by heart could read the page. A stranger could not.

Muslim tradition tells how the marks were added. A grammarian of Basra named Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali (d. c. 688) is credited with the first system: colored dots placed to show vowels. In the time of the governor al-Hajjaj (c. 700), two of his students are said to have added dots to distinguish the consonants. Later, al-Khalil ibn Ahmad (d. c. 786), the founder of Arabic dictionary-making, designed the small strokes and marks for vowels still used today.

Historians note that the details of these stories are uncertain. Manuscripts show the changes happening gradually over a century or more. What is certain is the direction. The script began as a bare memory aid. It became a fully marked script that anyone who knew Arabic could read. Printed copies today show every dot and every vowel. They even mark where to pause and how long to hold a sound.

This history explains something students notice: why a Qur'an page looks so different from an Arabic newspaper. The newspaper leaves out the short vowels, since fluent readers do not need them. The Qur'an keeps every mark, because getting a single sound wrong in recitation matters to Muslims. The page is designed so the voice can be exact.

words.d: small signs above and below Arabic letters showing short vowels; added to Qur'an copies in the first Islamic centuries
a grammarian of Basra (d. c. 688) credited by tradition with the first vowel-marking system
a scholar of Basra (d. c. 786) credited with the vowel signs used in Arabic today

look.title: Reading Without Vowels
look.text: Try this English sentence with the vowels removed: 'Th ct st n th mt.' A reader who has heard 'The cat sat on the mat' many times reads it at once. A reader who has not could get 'The cot sat in the mit' or something else. Early Arabic script worked something like this, and had shared letter shapes as well.
look.prompt: Who could read the early bare script well, and who could not? What does that tell you about who the first written copies were for?

check.q: Why could early Qur'an manuscripts be read by some people and not others?
choices: They lacked dots and vowel marks, so a reader needed to know the text already
check.why: The bare early script was a memory aid; those who knew the text could read it, strangers could not.

check.q: Who does tradition credit with the vowel signs used in Arabic today?
check.why: Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad (d. c. 786) is credited with designing the marks still in use.

check.q: Why does a printed Qur'an show every vowel mark when an Arabic newspaper does not?
choices: Because Muslims want recitation to be exact in every sound
Because the Qur'an is in a different language
Because the marks were added in 1924
check.why: Fluent readers skip short vowels in ordinary text, but the Qur'an is marked fully so it can be recited exactly.

lessons.title: The Readings: Hafs and Warsh
lessons.mainIdea: Within the Uthmanic text, Muslim scholars recognize several accepted ways of reciting, the qira'at; most of the world uses the reading of Hafs, and North and West Africa use Warsh.
reading: The Uthmanic text fixed the letters but not every sound. Small differences in vowels, in lengthening, and occasionally in a word remained among the teachers of recitation in different cities. These traditions of recitation are called *qira'at*, readings. Each is passed from teacher to student in a chain going back, Muslims say, to the companions of the Prophet. A hadith says the Qur'an was revealed in seven ahruf, or modes, which scholars connect to this variety in different ways.

In the tenth century, a scholar in Baghdad named Ibn Mujahid (d. 936) selected seven readings as authoritative, one from each of the main cities: Medina, Mecca, Damascus, Basra and three from Kufa. Later scholars accepted three more, making ten. Each reading is named for a master reciter and is known through two of his students. The reading of Asim of Kufa, as transmitted by his student *Hafs* (d. c. 796), is one of the seven.

Today the reading of Hafs is used by the great majority of Muslims, from Turkey to Indonesia to Chicago. The reading of Nafi of Medina, as transmitted by his student *Warsh* (d. c. 812), is common in Morocco, Algeria and parts of West Africa. Copies of the Qur'an are printed in each. The differences are mostly in pronunciation. A small number affect the sense of a word, and commentators discuss those cases.

For Muslims, the readings are not rival Qur'ans. They are accepted ways of sounding one text, all going back to the Prophet's teaching, in the tradition's view. Historians see in them the traces of the regional teaching that the early script allowed. Both agree the readings are old, limited and carefully recorded. A trained reciter can often tell you which reading is being used within a few verses.

words.d: the accepted readings, or ways of reciting, the Qur'an; seven were fixed in the tenth century, later ten
transmitter (d. c. 796) of the reading of Asim of Kufa; the reading most Muslims use today
transmitter (d. c. 812) of the reading of Nafi of Medina; used in North and West Africa
Baghdad scholar (d. 936) who selected the seven authoritative readings

look.title: One Text, Two Sounds
look.text: In Qur'an 1:4, most copies read 'maliki,' 'Owner' or 'Master' of the Day of Judgment; some accepted readings have 'maliki' with a short vowel, 'King.' Pickthall translated 'Owner.' Rodwell wrote 'King.' Both words fit the same letters on the Uthmanic page. Commentators say both meanings are true of God, in the Muslim view, and the readings keep both.
look.prompt: The letters are the same and the vowel differs. How does that one small difference show why vowel marks and chains of teachers both matter?

check.q: What are the qira'at?
choices: accepted ways of reciting the one Uthmanic text
the thirty parts of the Qur'an
check.why: Qira'at are readings, traditions of recitation passed through chains of teachers.

check.q: Which reading do most Muslims in the world use today?
check.why: The reading of Hafs is used across most of the Muslim world; Warsh is common in North and West Africa.

check.q: Who fixed the number of authoritative readings at seven?
choices: Ibn Mujahid in the tenth century
check.why: Ibn Mujahid (d. 936) selected seven readings; three more were later accepted.

lessons.title: The Rules of Tajwid
lessons.mainIdea: Tajwid is the set of rules for pronouncing the Qur'an exactly, learned from a teacher, so that every sound comes out as tradition says it should.
reading: *Tajwid* means to make something good or beautiful. In Qur'an study it names the rules for correct recitation. The rules say where each sound is made in the mouth and throat. They say how long a vowel is held, when a sound is nasal, when two sounds merge, and where to pause. Muslim teachers tie it to Qur'an 73:4, which tells the Prophet to recite in slow, measured tones. Scholars described the rules from the ninth century on. They are taught the same way today.

Some rules a beginner meets early. *Madd* is lengthening: certain long vowels are held for two, four or six counts, and printed copies mark them with a small wavy sign. *Ghunnah* is a nasal hum on certain n and m sounds. *Idgham* is merging one letter into the next. *Qalqalah* is a slight echo on five letters when they close a syllable. Each rule has a name and a sign or a place on the page.

Tajwid is learned by ear from a teacher, then checked by the page. A student recites. The teacher corrects. The student repeats. This is how the Qur'an has been passed on, Muslims say, since the Prophet taught his companions, in an unbroken chain of listening. A certificate that a student has recited the whole Qur'an correctly to a teacher is called an ijaza, and it lists the teacher's own chain of teachers.

Non-Arabic speakers learn tajwid too. Many Muslim children in Chicago speak Urdu, Bosnian, Somali or English at home. They attend weekend classes where they learn to sound the Arabic exactly. Often this comes before they know what the words mean. Muslims explain that the sound itself is the revealed form. Meaning is learned alongside it, not in place of it.

words.d: the rules for reciting the Qur'an correctly: where sounds are made, how long they are held, when they merge
lengthening of a vowel in recitation, held for a set number of counts
a nasal hum on certain n and m sounds in recitation
a certificate that a student has recited the Qur'an correctly to a teacher, listing the chain of teachers

look.title: In Measured Tones
look.text: The Qur'an tells the Prophet to stand in prayer through part of the night and to recite the Qur'an in slow, measured, distinct tones. Muslim teachers of tajwid cite this verse as the root of their art.
look.cite: Qur'an 73:4, Surah Al-Muzzammil (The Enshrouded One), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Why might a tradition that values exact sound build a whole set of rules from a verse that says 'recite in measured tones'?

check.q: What does tajwid cover?
choices: the rules for pronouncing and pacing recitation
check.why: Tajwid is the science of correct recitation: sounds, lengths, merges and pauses.

check.q: What is madd?
choices: a pause at the end of a verse
lengthening a vowel for a set number of counts
check.why: Madd is lengthening; ghunnah is the nasal sound; idgham is merging.

check.q: How is tajwid mainly passed on?
choices: from a teacher by ear, then checked against the page
by reading a printed rulebook alone
check.why: A student recites to a teacher who corrects, in a chain Muslims trace back to the Prophet.

lessons.title: The Cairo Edition
lessons.mainIdea: In 1924 a committee in Cairo printed a carefully checked Qur'an in the Hafs reading; it became the model for most printed copies in the world.
reading: Printing came late to the Qur'an. Muslims long preferred hand-copied mushafs, partly out of respect and partly because early printed Arabic was ugly and full of errors. A Venice printing of about 1537 is thought to have failed for that reason. Printed Qur'ans made by Muslims appeared in St. Petersburg in 1787 and later in India and Istanbul, but they varied in spelling and verse numbering from press to press.

In Egypt, a committee of scholars from al-Azhar, the great teaching mosque of Cairo, set out to produce one authoritative printed text. They worked from the reading of Hafs from Asim and from the classical books on spelling and verse counting. The result appeared in 1924 under King Fuad I and is known as the *Cairo edition* or the King Fuad edition. It uses the Kufan verse count, giving 6,236 ayahs.

The Cairo edition did not create a new text. Its aim was to print the Uthmanic text in the Hafs reading with full tajwid marks, standard spelling and clear surah headings, including the traditional Meccan or Medinan label and the chronological number. Because it was careful and widely accepted, later presses copied it. The Medina printing complex in Saudi Arabia, which has printed hundreds of millions of copies since 1985, follows the same text.

Historians call 1924 a turning point. For the first time, most Muslims in the world could hold an identical printed page. Scholars in universities use the Cairo verse numbers too. So a citation like 2:255 means the same thing everywhere. Older European translations, including Rodwell's of 1861, sometimes use a different verse count. That is why a reference can be off by one or two when you compare them.

words.d: the printed Qur'an of 1924, prepared at al-Azhar in the Hafs reading; the model for most printed copies
the mosque and university in Cairo, founded in the tenth century, whose scholars prepared the 1924 edition
the system of numbering verses used in the Cairo edition, giving 6,236 ayahs

check.why: The Cairo edition prints the Hafs reading with the Kufan verse count.

check.q: Why can a verse number in Rodwell's 1861 translation differ from a modern citation?
choices: Rodwell's edition used a different verse count than the 1924 Cairo edition

choices: to print the Uthmanic text in one careful, standard form
check.why: The Cairo edition did not create a new text; it standardized spelling, marks and numbering in print.

lessons.title: Sound First, Still Today
lessons.mainIdea: Even with printed and digital copies everywhere, Muslims still treat the Qur'an as sound first: memorized, recited aloud and heard.
reading: Everything in this chapter, the collection, the dots, the readings, the printing, served one goal in Muslim eyes: keeping the recited word exact. The Qur'an says of itself that God sent down the Reminder and will guard it (15:9). Muslims read this as a promise that the text will be preserved. Historians describe the same result in different words: a text kept by memory and writing together, with unusual care, from a very early date.

The proof, Muslims often say, is the huffaz. Today millions of people, children and adults, on every continent, have memorized the entire Qur'an. Competitions are held each year in which young reciters from dozens of countries are judged on memory and tajwid. In Ramadan, mosques from Jakarta to Chicago hear the whole book recited over the month. If every printed copy vanished, the tradition says, the text would survive in voices, as it did at first.

Technology has followed the sound. Famous reciters such as Abdul Basit Abdus Samad and Mahmoud Khalil al-Husary were recorded in Egypt in the twentieth century. Their recordings are still listened to daily. Apps show the text with each word highlighted as a reciter reads it, in Hafs or in Warsh. A student in Illinois can hear the same recitation a student in Cairo hears. That is what Uthman's copies were meant to secure, in a form he could not have imagined.

For a public-school reader, the takeaway is not about belief. It is about how a text can be kept. The Qur'an is a case study in transmission by voice and page together, checked against each other for fourteen centuries, and now checked, too, against parchment in laboratories. Knowing how it got from a cave near Mecca to a phone in your pocket is knowing something real about the book.

words.d: how a text is passed on over time, by memory, copying, printing or recording
a person trained to recite the Qur'an aloud according to tajwid; famous reciters are recorded and studied

look.title: We Are Its Guardian
look.text: Lo! We, even We, reveal the Reminder, and lo! We verily are its Guardian.
look.cite: Qur'an 15:9, Surah Al-Hijr, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Muslims read this verse as a promise that the text is preserved. A historian would describe the preservation without the promise. Write one sentence in each voice.

check.q: How do Muslims read Qur'an 15:9?
choices: as a promise that God preserves the text
as a list of the readings
as a description of the Cairo edition
check.why: The verse says God sent down the Reminder and guards it; Muslims take it as a promise of preservation.

check.q: Which of these is a famous twentieth-century reciter?
check.why: Abdul Basit, an Egyptian reciter, was recorded in the twentieth century; the others are a scholar, a scribe and a historian.

check.q: What is transmission, in the study of a text?
choices: how the text is passed on over time by memory, copying, printing or recording
check.why: Transmission covers every way a text travels from its first form to later readers.

review.q: What does the word Qur'an mean?
review.why: Qur'an comes from a root meaning to recite; the written copy is called a mushaf.

review.q: Under which caliph does tradition say the first collection into sheets was made?
review.why: Abu Bakr had Zayd ibn Thabit gather the text after the battle of Yamama, c. 633.

choices: sent standard copies to the main cities and ordered other versions destroyed
review.why: The Uthmanic codex gave the text one written form across the growing Muslim world.

review.q: The Birmingham leaves were radiocarbon-dated to which range?
review.why: The 2015 result was 568 to 645 CE with 95.4 percent probability; 649 to 675 is the Tübingen folio.

choices: a page written over an erased earlier text
review.why: The Sana'a palimpsest has an early variant Qur'an under a standard one.

review.q: Why were dots and vowel marks added to the Arabic script?
choices: to make the pages look prettier
so readers who did not already know the text could read it correctly
review.why: The bare early script served memorizers; marks let any Arabic reader recite exactly.

choices: the way of reciting used by most Muslims today
review.why: Hafs from Asim of Kufa is the reading used across most of the Muslim world and in the Cairo edition.

choices: Ibn Mujahid fixed the seven readings
A standard printed Qur'an was issued that most later copies follow
review.why: The Cairo (King Fuad) edition, in the Hafs reading with the Kufan count, became the model for printing.
